  And one mistake of mine that a subagent caught. Re-stamping the migration during the merge, I rebuilt its snapshot by hand and checked the wrong key
  for check constraints, silently dropping 'labels' from a constraint the database has had for days.

  Technical health

  Good, and better than when this started. The migration-watermark hazard is closed properly rather than worked around. The cascade test is now
  derived from the schema, so a fifteenth foreign key goes red instead of passing silently. The one piece of debt I'm carrying deliberately is
  deleteTerminalJobs inheriting an exposure that trimFinished has always had — a terminal job with an unsettled reservation is possible in the
  database even though no application path produces one. I've asked for a cheap guard, with instructions to stop and report rather than build it if it
  needs a schema change.

  What's left, and what it costs

  1. The two fix passes now running, then a narrowly scoped third check on each — not general discovery, which closed at round two.
  2. npm run check on a settled tree. The last run was red on two gates and couldn't attribute the failure, because three agents had uncommitted work
     in the tree.
  3. Push to dev. Half a day, most of it review latency rather than typing.
  4. Not the routes.ts immutable cache-header item, and not the "Not shared" wording a deleted article's URL shows its own owner. Both recorded for
     you.

  Cost/benefit

  Still clearly worth it — and the shape of the spend has been reviews, not construction. A–D delivers what a reader recognises: the article is gone,
  the shelf is right, the bill is right.

  Stage E remains most of the remaining cost and none of the visible value. You confirmed it once with the cost visible, so I'm not reopening it — but
  it wants its own plan doc rather than being the tail of this one. I'll give you the full explanation of why it's a lot of work when A–D is pushed,
  as you asked.

✻ Waiting for 2 background agents to finish
